title: Build a Complete React Application
subtitle: A short practical refresher followed by 20 new application questions
description: Review the ten React Development dashboard topics. Includes three capstone examples and exactly two fresh review questions from each of Lessons 1–10.

blocks.text: Welcome to the React Development final review. This lesson is intentionally shorter on new theory and longer on practical decisions. You will revisit the ten dashboard topics and answer two new application questions for each lesson, for exactly 20 questions.

Start by reading the requirement, tracing where its data comes from, and deciding what success should look like. Then test both a normal case and a boundary or failure case. A correct program should not only work once; it should behave predictably when its inputs change.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select React Development. Paste this snippet into the matching web/React editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Capstone sample 1: Build a Complete React Application

blocks.text: The first sample illustrates a small part of the solution. Before extending it, separate the input, the transformation, and the output. That separation makes it easier to test each part and locate defects.

A final project combines several ideas instead of treating each lesson as an isolated trick. Keep the responsibilities clear, choose data structures that match the job, and validate information at the boundary where it enters the program.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select React Development. Paste this snippet into the matching web/React editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Capstone sample 3: Build a Complete React Application

blocks.text: Use the third example as a starting point, then explain how it relates to the course topic: Bring components, JSX, props, state, hooks, events, data and routing together in a complete React development project.

Answer two questions from each dashboard lesson. These questions are newly written for this review and are not copied from the corresponding lesson quizzes. Read carefully: select the option that best satisfies the requirement, not merely an option that could work in a different situation.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 1 — Introduction to React: A team receives a repository with no run instructions. What should the maintainer add to make a fresh setup verifiable?
options: A setup/run guide plus a minimal test or sample command.
Only a screenshot of the editor.
A statement that setup is obvious.
blocks.explanation: A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 1 — Introduction to React: The app works after manual edits but fails when built from source. What should be compared?
options: The actual source, compiler/runtime configuration, and documented build path.
blocks.explanation: Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 2 — JSX and Components: A component needs to render a list of elements conditionally. What should it return?
options: A valid JSX element tree with branches/collections mapped to elements.
A CSS file as a value.
Two adjacent root elements with no wrapper in all cases.
A string of untrusted HTML by default.
blocks.explanation: A React component should return a valid element tree and can use conditional expressions to choose content.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A React component should return a valid element tree and can use conditional expressions to choose content.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A React component should return a valid element tree and can use conditional expressions to choose content.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 2 — JSX and Components: A standard HTML class attribute is written in JSX. What spelling should be used?
blocks.explanation: React JSX uses className.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. React JSX uses className.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. React JSX uses className.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 3 — Props and Component Communication: A reusable card must display different titles without editing the component. What is the best approach?
blocks.explanation: Props configure reusable components with different input data.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Props configure reusable components with different input data.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Props configure reusable components with different input data.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 3 — Props and Component Communication: The child needs to request a parent-managed update. What interface commonly supports this?
options: Write to the parent’s variable directly.
Change the child’s prop value in place.
Receive a callback prop and invoke it.
blocks.explanation: Callback props let children signal events to parents while preserving one owner for state.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Callback props let children signal events to parents while preserving one owner for state.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Callback props let children signal events to parents while preserving one owner for state.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 4 — State and User Interaction: A state array changes but React does not show the update because the original array was mutated. What is the safer update?
options: Create a new array with the desired change.
Write the new text directly to the DOM.
Refresh the browser after every click.
blocks.explanation: Immutable updates create a new reference and keep state changes predictable.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Immutable updates create a new reference and keep state changes predictable.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Immutable updates create a new reference and keep state changes predictable.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 4 — State and User Interaction: A total can be computed from state values. What generally avoids unnecessary synchronization?
options: Keep a separate total and update it in every handler.
Derive the total when rendering if the calculation is inexpensive.
Use a side effect for all math.
blocks.explanation: Derived values reduce duplicated state and avoid inconsistencies.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Derived values reduce duplicated state and avoid inconsistencies.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Derived values reduce duplicated state and avoid inconsistencies.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 5 — React Hooks: An effect adds a listener to window. What must be considered?
options: Whether the listener should run forever.
Dependency correctness and cleanup when it is no longer needed.
Whether the JSX contains a table.
blocks.explanation: Effects synchronize with external systems; cleanup prevents stale listeners and leaks.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Effects synchronize with external systems; cleanup prevents stale listeners and leaks.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Effects synchronize with external systems; cleanup prevents stale listeners and leaks.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 5 — React Hooks: A useState call is inside a loop. Why is that invalid?
options: Hooks must be called at the component/custom-hook top level in a stable order.
blocks.explanation: React relies on a stable call order for hooks across renders.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. React relies on a stable call order for hooks across renders.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. React relies on a stable call order for hooks across renders.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 6 — Forms and Events: A controlled input’s value never changes as the user types. Which piece is likely missing?
options: A change handler that updates the state used for value.
blocks.explanation: The controlled field’s displayed value comes from state, so the change handler must update it.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The controlled field’s displayed value comes from state, so the change handler must update it.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. The controlled field’s displayed value comes from state, so the change handler must update it.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 6 — Forms and Events: A form validates successfully in the browser. Should a trusted server skip validation?
options: Yes, every browser request is safe.
No; enforce the validation and authorization at the server/data boundary too.
Only if the form is React.
Only if the user uses a phone.
blocks.explanation: Browser checks improve usability but can be bypassed.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Browser checks improve usability but can be bypassed.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Browser checks improve usability but can be bypassed.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 7 — Lists, Conditional Rendering and Data: A list item has a key based on its index, but items can be reordered and retain component state. What should be used?
options: The array length for every item.
A stable identifier tied to each item.
A random new key on every render.
blocks.explanation: Stable identity lets React associate state and DOM with the correct item when ordering changes.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Stable identity lets React associate state and DOM with the correct item when ordering changes.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Stable identity lets React associate state and DOM with the correct item when ordering changes.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 7 — Lists, Conditional Rendering and Data: A request succeeded but returned an empty array. What should the UI communicate?
options: Show an error even though none occurred.
An empty state distinct from loading and error.
blocks.explanation: Loading, empty, and error states mean different things to users.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Loading, empty, and error states mean different things to users.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Loading, empty, and error states mean different things to users.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 8 — React Routing and Application Structure: A protected React route hides its menu link but data remains publicly readable. What is required?
blocks.explanation: UI hiding is not authorization; access must be enforced where the data is protected.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. UI hiding is not authorization; access must be enforced where the data is protected.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. UI hiding is not authorization; access must be enforced where the data is protected.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 8 — React Routing and Application Structure: A user refreshes /lessons/3 and the host returns 404 before React loads. What should be configured?
options: An event handler on every paragraph.
blocks.explanation: Single-page application hosting typically needs a rule that serves the app entry for client routes.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Single-page application hosting typically needs a rule that serves the app entry for client routes.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Single-page application hosting typically needs a rule that serves the app entry for client routes.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 9 — Advanced React Patterns: An object’s internal data can be changed into impossible combinations by any caller. What design improvement addresses that?
options: Encapsulate state and expose validated operations.
blocks.explanation: Encapsulation helps enforce invariants across every caller.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Encapsulation helps enforce invariants across every caller.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Encapsulation helps enforce invariants across every caller.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 9 — Advanced React Patterns: A design uses deep inheritance to share one small helper. What alternative should be evaluated?
options: Composition or a small interface when the relationship is not truly “is-a.”
blocks.explanation: Composition can reuse behavior without forcing an incorrect type relationship.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Composition can reuse behavior without forcing an incorrect type relationship.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Composition can reuse behavior without forcing an incorrect type relationship.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 10 — Build a Complete React Application: The final project passes one example input. What is the strongest completion check?
options: Stop testing as soon as the screen appears.
Remove error handling to reduce lines.
Test normal, boundary, empty, and failure cases and document how to run it.
blocks.explanation: Broader tests and reproducible setup provide stronger evidence than one happy-path example.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Broader tests and reproducible setup provide stronger evidence than one happy-path example.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Broader tests and reproducible setup provide stronger evidence than one happy-path example.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 10 — Build a Complete React Application: A teammate cannot reproduce the project’s behavior. What is likely missing?
options: Repeatable instructions, clear dependencies, and a testable expected result.
blocks.explanation: Reproducibility requires enough source and setup information for another person to verify the same behavior.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Reproducibility requires enough source and setup information for another person to verify the same behavior.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Reproducibility requires enough source and setup information for another person to verify the same behavior.
